facts.fact: On a standard 400-metre outdoor track, the 800 metres is exactly two laps, so runners plan the race as a first lap and a second lap.
facts.hook: a runner loses count and kicks for the finish one lap too early

facts.fact: In the 800 metres on an outdoor track, runners must stay in their own lanes until a breakline after the first bend; cutting in before it gets a runner disqualified.
facts.hook: a nervous first-timer nearly cuts to the inside lane straight off the start

facts.fact: Because 800-metre runners stay in lanes around the first bend, they start from staggered positions, with outer lanes placed farther ahead so everyone runs the same distance.
facts.hook: a runner in lane six complains the others got a head start

facts.fact: A split is the time for one section of a race; an 800-metre runner's 400-metre split shows right away whether the first lap was faster or slower than planned.
facts.hook: a coach shouts a lap time that is far too fast

facts.fact: To finish 800 metres in three minutes on a 400-metre track, a runner must average 90 seconds for each lap.
facts.hook: working out a lap target on the back of a race number

facts.fact: Running the second half of a race faster than the first is called a negative split; running the first half faster is called a positive split.
facts.hook: two teammates compare their lap times after the same race

facts.fact: When David Rudisha set the men's 800-metre world record at the 2012 London Olympics, his first lap was more than two seconds faster than his second.
facts.hook: a runner watches the record race to see how a champion paced it

facts.fact: One lap in lane two of a standard track is about 7.67 metres longer than in lane one, so running wide around the bends on the outside of a pack costs extra distance.
facts.hook: a runner passes on the bend and wonders why the finish feels farther

facts.fact: The 800 metres draws on aerobic energy, which uses oxygen, and anaerobic energy, which works without oxygen but runs out quickly, so it feels like a sprint and a distance race at once.
facts.hook: a sprinter and a distance runner both try the 800 for the first time

facts.fact: Sprinting the first lap faster than a pace you can hold uses up quick anaerobic energy early, so the runner usually slows sharply on the second lap.
facts.hook: the early leader fades and gets passed on the final straight

facts.fact: In track races a bell rings as the leader starts the final lap, so in the 800 metres the bell sounds when the leader reaches the halfway point.
facts.hook: a runner hears the bell and realizes there is still a whole lap left

facts.fact: Running directly behind another runner shelters you from the wind, so following someone on the first lap can save energy for the finish.
facts.hook: tucking in behind a rival on a windy back straight

facts.fact: Every extra character multiplies the number of possible passwords: using only lowercase letters, adding one more letter makes 26 times as many possibilities to guess.
facts.hook: a friend insists their six-letter password is long enough

facts.fact: The US standards agency NIST says a password that is the only thing protecting an account should be at least 15 characters long.
facts.hook: a sign-up form accepts an 8-character password and a cousin says that is too short

facts.fact: NIST's password guidance tells systems not to require mixes of uppercase letters, numbers and symbols, because length adds more strength than those rules do.
facts.hook: arguing with a website that demands a symbol in the password

facts.fact: NIST's guidance says systems should not force people to change passwords on a schedule, only when there is evidence a password has been stolen.
facts.hook: a parent's office makes everyone pick a new password every month

facts.fact: A passphrase of several random words, like the 2011 xkcd comic's example 'correct horse battery staple', is long enough to be hard to guess yet easy to remember.
facts.hook: making up a silly four-word password that nobody could guess

facts.fact: In credential stuffing, attackers take usernames and passwords leaked from one site and try them automatically on many other sites, so one reused password can unlock several accounts.
facts.hook: a game account gets hacked after a different website had a breach

facts.fact: Have I Been Pwned, a website launched by security researcher Troy Hunt in December 2013, lets people check whether their email address appeared in a known data breach.
facts.hook: checking a grandparent's email and finding it in an old breach

facts.fact: Password-guessing programs try dictionary words, names, and common swaps like '@' for 'a' or '0' for 'o' early, so those swaps add little strength.
facts.hook: a friend proudly shows off 'p@ssw0rd' as their clever password

facts.fact: Birthdays, pet names and favourite teams make weak passwords because they can often be found on a person's social media.
facts.hook: someone guesses a classmate's password from their profile page

facts.fact: Well-run websites store a hash of each password, a scrambled one-way fingerprint, instead of the password itself, so they can check a login without keeping the real password.
facts.hook: a repair shop worker explains why the site cannot tell you your old password

facts.fact: A password manager creates a different random password for every site and locks them all behind one master password, so a person only has to remember one.
facts.hook: a grandparent's notebook of passwords gets replaced by an app

facts.fact: Two-factor authentication asks for a second proof, such as a code sent to a phone, so a stolen password on its own is not enough to log in.
facts.hook: a login attempt from another country is stopped by a code request

facts.fact: A pivot table summarises a long list of rows by grouping them, for example turning hundreds of survey responses into one row per grade.
facts.hook: a student council drowning in survey answers needs one clear summary

facts.fact: In Excel, the PivotTable Fields pane has four areas, Filters, Columns, Rows and Values, and dragging a field into an area decides where it appears in the table.
facts.hook: dragging fields around until the survey summary finally makes sense

facts.fact: Putting the Grade field in a pivot table's Rows area lists each different grade once down the left side of the table.
facts.hook: a list of 400 answers collapses into three neat grade rows

facts.fact: With Grade in Rows, Answer in Columns and Answer again in Values as a count, a pivot table shows how many students in each grade gave each answer.
facts.hook: finding out which grade actually voted for the later lunch

facts.fact: In Excel, a field placed in the Values area is summed by default if it holds only numbers, but counted if it contains any text or blank cells.
facts.hook: a pivot table shows counts instead of totals because of one blank cell

facts.fact: A pivot table's summary can be switched from Sum or Count to Average, turning a column of one-to-five ratings into the mean rating for each grade.
facts.hook: comparing how much each grade liked the field trip

facts.fact: Excel's 'Show Values As' option can display each count as a percentage of its column or row total, so grades with different numbers of students can be compared fairly.
facts.hook: the biggest grade seems to win every question until percentages are shown

facts.fact: A pivot table uses each column heading as a field name, so survey data needs one header row with a label at the top of every column.
facts.hook: Excel refuses to build the pivot table because a column has no heading

facts.fact: A pivot table treats 'Gr 7' and 'Grade 7' as two separate groups, so answers must be typed consistently before they are summarised.
facts.hook: grade seven appears twice in the summary with half its votes each time

facts.fact: Empty cells in the column being grouped appear in an Excel pivot table as their own group labelled '(blank)'.
facts.hook: a mystery '(blank)' grade turns out to be students who skipped the question

facts.fact: Slicers, clickable buttons that filter a pivot table, were added to Excel in Excel 2010.
facts.hook: clicking a grade button to show only that grade's answers

facts.fact: Pito Salas, working on the spreadsheet program Lotus Improv, released in 1991, is credited with inventing the pivot table.
facts.hook: a parent at the office remembers when pivot tables were brand new

facts.fact: Google marks paid search results with the label 'Sponsored' so they can be told apart from ordinary results.
facts.hook: a grandparent clicks the first link, not noticing the Sponsored label

facts.fact: Paid ads often appear at the very top of a search results page, above the unpaid results, so the first link is not necessarily the most useful one.
facts.hook: the top result for a free homework tool asks for a credit card

facts.fact: Unpaid search results are called organic results, and Google says advertisers cannot pay to move their pages higher in them.
facts.hook: a friend thinks the top real result must have paid to be there

facts.fact: Advertisers bid in an auction for search keywords and usually pay only when someone clicks their ad, a system called pay-per-click.
facts.hook: a shop owner explains why every click on their ad costs money

facts.fact: In 2013 the US Federal Trade Commission told search engines that paid results must be clearly distinguishable from natural results, or they risk deceiving users.
facts.hook: a class debates whether an ad disguised as a result is fair

facts.fact: Putting quotation marks around a phrase asks Google to find pages containing those exact words in that exact order.
facts.hook: searching for a half-remembered song lyric in quotes

facts.fact: A minus sign placed directly before a word, with no space, removes results containing that word, so jaguar -car finds the animal instead of the car.
facts.hook: a jaguar project buried under car dealership results

facts.fact: The site: operator limits a search to one website or domain ending, so adding site:.gov shows only pages from US government websites.
facts.hook: looking for official weather warnings instead of rumor sites

facts.fact: Web addresses ending in .edu can be registered only by accredited colleges and universities in the United States.
facts.hook: trusting a source a little more after noticing its web address

facts.fact: In Google, the word OR between two search words must be typed in capital letters to find pages containing either word.
facts.hook: a search for 'cats or dogs' does not work the way a kid expected

facts.fact: Google founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin ranked web pages partly by how many other pages linked to them, a method called PageRank after Page.
facts.hook: wondering why a popular site always shows up first

facts.fact: Specific keywords like 'bike chain slips when pedalling uphill' narrow results to pages about the actual problem, while a vague search like 'bike problem' returns mostly unrelated pages.
facts.hook: fixing a bike at a friend's house with a better search

facts.fact: Every formula in Excel or Google Sheets begins with an equals sign; without it, the cell just shows what was typed as text.
facts.hook: a total that shows 'SUM(B2:B10)' instead of a number

facts.fact: The formula =SUM(B2:B10) adds every cell from B2 to B10; the colon between the two cells marks a range.
facts.hook: adding up the week's lemonade sales in one step

facts.fact: A spreadsheet cell's address is its column letter followed by its row number, so C4 is the cell in column C, row 4.
facts.hook: a friend reads out the wrong cell over the phone

facts.fact: When a number inside a summed range changes, the SUM formula recalculates the total automatically.
facts.hook: fixing one typo and watching the total update by itself

facts.fact: Copying =SUM(B2:B10) one column to the right turns it into =SUM(C2:C10), because ordinary cell references are relative and shift with the formula.
facts.hook: one formula copied across the row totals every column at once

facts.fact: In Excel, pressing Alt and the equals sign together inserts an AutoSum formula that adds the numbers next to the selected cell.
facts.hook: a parent at the office shows a shortcut that saves typing

facts.fact: SUM skips cells that hold text, so a number stored as text is silently left out of the total.
facts.hook: a column total comes out too small because one number was pasted as text

facts.fact: A formula that includes its own cell, such as =SUM(B2:B10) typed into cell B10, is called a circular reference, and Excel warns about it.
facts.hook: a warning pops up after typing the total in the wrong cell

facts.fact: In Excel, a 'bar chart' has horizontal bars and a 'column chart' has vertical bars, although both compare amounts across categories.
facts.hook: the chart comes out sideways because the wrong type was picked

facts.fact: A bar chart whose value axis starts above zero makes small differences look much bigger than they really are.
facts.hook: a chart makes one team's slight lead look enormous

facts.fact: VisiCalc, written by Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston and released for the Apple II in 1979, was the first spreadsheet program for personal computers.
facts.hook: a grandparent remembers doing sums on the first home spreadsheet

facts.fact: William Playfair published the first known bar chart in 1786, in his Commercial and Political Atlas, showing Scotland's imports and exports.
facts.hook: learning the bar chart is older than the light bulb

facts.fact: In Python, input() always returns text, even when the user types digits, so the answer must be converted with int() before it can be multiplied as a number.
facts.hook: a times-table program that prints nonsense for the number 7

facts.fact: In Python, multiplying text by a whole number repeats the text, so '7' * 3 gives '777' instead of 21.
facts.hook: the program prints 777 and the coding club laughs

facts.fact: In Python, range(1, 11) produces the numbers 1 to 10, stopping just before its second number, so a table up to 12 needs range(1, 13).
facts.hook: the times table mysteriously stops at 11

facts.fact: A Python for loop runs its indented block once for each value, so for i in range(1, 11) runs the multiplication line ten times.
facts.hook: replacing ten copied print lines with one loop

facts.fact: Python uses indentation to show which lines belong inside a loop; a line that is not indented runs only once, after the loop has finished.
facts.hook: only the last row of the table prints

facts.fact: If the user types a word such as 'seven', Python's int() raises a ValueError, and the program stops unless the error is handled.
facts.hook: a grandparent types the number in words and crashes the program

facts.fact: A Python f-string such as f"{n} x {i} = {n * i}" places the values of variables and calculations directly into the printed text.
facts.hook: making each line of the table read like a real times table

facts.fact: Python variable names are case-sensitive, so Number and number are two different variables.
facts.hook: a NameError caused by one capital letter

facts.fact: Python's print() starts a new line after each output by default; adding end=' ' keeps the next output on the same line.
facts.hook: trying to fit the whole table into one row

facts.fact: A while loop repeats as long as its condition is true, so a loop whose condition never becomes false runs forever until someone stops the program.
facts.hook: a camp laptop fills its screen with endless output

facts.fact: Guido van Rossum began creating Python in December 1989 and first published its code in February 1991.
facts.hook: a club leader tells how old the language really is

facts.fact: The Python programming language is named after the BBC comedy show Monty Python's Flying Circus, not after the snake.
facts.hook: a kid designs a snake logo for the club and gets corrected

facts.fact: The CSS rule h1 { text-align: center; } centres the text of every top-level heading on the page.
facts.hook: a homepage heading stuck against the left edge

facts.fact: CSS uses the American spelling, so the browser ignores text-align: centre; only text-align: center works.
facts.hook: a Canadian kid's heading refuses to move until the spelling changes

facts.fact: HTML has six levels of headings, h1 to h6, with h1 the most important.
facts.hook: choosing which heading tag to use for the page title

facts.fact:
Most HTML tags come in pairs: an opening tag like

and a closing tag with a slash,

, wrapped around the content.
facts.hook: the whole page turns into a giant heading because of a missing slash

facts.fact: A heading is a block element that stretches across the full width of its container, which is why text-align: center puts its text in the middle of the page.
facts.hook: wondering where the middle is before the heading moves

facts.fact: The old <center> tag was deprecated in HTML 4 in favour of the CSS text-align property.
facts.hook: a grandparent's old web tutorial uses a tag that is out of date

facts.fact: A CSS rule has a selector followed by curly braces holding properties and values, with each declaration ending in a semicolon.
facts.hook: a missing semicolon breaks every style after it

facts.fact: An external stylesheet is connected to a web page by a link tag with rel="stylesheet" placed inside the page's head section.
facts.hook: styles in style.css do nothing until the page is linked to them

facts.fact: When two CSS rules of equal specificity set the same property, the one written later wins; this ordering is part of the cascade in Cascading Style Sheets.
facts.hook: a heading keeps going back to the left because of a rule lower down

facts.fact: Starting a file with <!DOCTYPE html> tells the browser the page is written in modern HTML, HTML5.
facts.hook: a page looks strange in the browser until the first line is added

facts.fact: Tim Berners-Lee created HTML while working at CERN, specifying it and writing the first web browser and server software in late 1990.
facts.hook: a camp counselor explains who wrote the first web page

facts.fact: Hakon Wium Lie proposed CSS on 10 October 1994, while working at CERN with Tim Berners-Lee.
facts.hook: learning that styling web pages came years after the web itself

facts.fact: Scratch, a block-based programming language, was developed at the MIT Media Lab and first released in 2007.
facts.hook: a grandparent is surprised coding can be done by snapping blocks

facts.fact: Scratch is named after DJ scratching, where a record is moved back and forth on a turntable to remix sounds.
facts.hook: a kid mixes sounds and code in the same game

facts.fact: To keep score in Scratch, a game makes a variable called score, sets it to 0 when the green flag is clicked, and uses 'change score by 1' for each point.
facts.hook: building the first game that actually counts points

facts.fact: A Scratch variable keeps its value between runs, so if the score is never set to 0 at the start, a new game begins with the old total.
facts.hook: a new player starts with 57 points and cries foul

facts.fact: An 'if touching' block placed outside any loop runs only once when the script starts; inside a 'forever' loop it is checked again and again.
facts.hook: the coin never gets collected even when the cat walks over it

facts.fact: If an 'if touching' block inside a forever loop adds a point and nothing moves the sprites apart, the score keeps rising for as long as they touch.
facts.hook: one coin is worth 200 points because it never disappears

facts.fact: In Scratch, a 'repeat 10' block runs the blocks inside it exactly ten times, while a 'forever' block keeps going until the program is stopped.
facts.hook: the enemy moves ten steps and then freezes

facts.fact: An 'if then else' block runs one set of blocks when its condition is true and a different set when it is false.
facts.hook: adding a lose message for when the player misses

facts.fact: A Scratch variable made 'for all sprites' can be used by every sprite, while one made 'for this sprite only' belongs to a single sprite.
facts.hook: the coin sprite cannot change the score the cat sprite made

facts.fact: Ticking the checkbox beside a Scratch variable shows a monitor on the stage, so players can watch the score change.
facts.hook: players cannot tell if they scored until the box is ticked

facts.fact: The Scratch stage is 480 by 360 pixels, with x running from -240 to 240 and y from -180 to 180, and the point (0, 0) at the centre.
facts.hook: a coin keeps appearing off the edge of the stage

facts.fact: In Scratch, clicking the green flag starts every script that begins with 'when green flag clicked', and the red stop sign stops all scripts.
facts.hook: a game that will not start because its script has no hat block

facts.fact: A prime number is a whole number greater than 1 whose only whole-number divisors are 1 and itself.
facts.hook: a coding club argues over whether 9 is prime

facts.fact: 1 is not a prime number; mathematicians exclude it so that every whole number has only one way to be written as a product of primes.
facts.hook: the program says 1 is prime and the leader asks why that is wrong

facts.fact: 2 is the only even prime number, because every larger even number can be divided evenly by 2.
facts.hook: a test run says 2 is not prime

facts.fact: In Python, the % operator gives the remainder of a division, so n % d == 0 is true exactly when d divides n evenly.
facts.hook: figuring out how a program can tell if a number divides evenly

facts.fact: To test whether n is prime, you only need to try divisors up to its square root, because if n is a times b, one of them is no bigger than that root.
facts.hook: a prime checker takes ages on a huge number until the loop is shortened

facts.fact: In Python, range(2, n) produces the numbers from 2 up to n minus 1, so it tries every possible divisor except 1 and n itself.
facts.hook: the checker says every number is not prime because it divides n by n

facts.fact: A break statement stops a loop immediately, so a prime checker can quit as soon as it finds a single divisor.
facts.hook: the program prints 'not prime' fifty times for one number

facts.fact: A Python for loop can have an else block that runs only if the loop finished without reaching break, which fits 'no divisor found, so the number is prime'.
facts.hook: a camp mentor shows a loop feature nobody at the table knew

facts.fact: A prime checker must handle numbers below 2 separately, because 0, 1 and negative numbers are not prime, yet a divisor loop starting at 2 finds nothing to reject them.
facts.hook: the program declares 0 a prime number

facts.fact: Around 300 BC, the Greek mathematician Euclid proved in his Elements that there are infinitely many prime numbers.
facts.hook: a kid hopes to find the biggest prime and learns there is none

facts.fact: The Sieve of Eratosthenes, an ancient Greek method, lists primes by crossing out the multiples of each prime in turn.
facts.hook: checking the program's answers against a hand-made grid

facts.fact: After checking whether a number is divisible by 2, a program only needs to test odd divisors, because an odd number can never be divided evenly by an even one.
facts.hook: halving the work of a slow prime checker

facts.fact: William Strunk Jr.'s writing guide The Elements of Style, written in 1918, gives the rule 'Omit needless words.'
facts.hook: a writing club member tapes the rule above their desk

facts.fact: Strunk wrote that a sentence should contain no unnecessary words for the same reason a drawing should have no unnecessary lines.
facts.hook: an artist friend explains cutting words like erasing stray pencil lines

facts.fact: The word 'revise' comes from the Latin revisere, meaning 'to look at again', since revising means seeing a draft with fresh eyes.
facts.hook: a student thinks revising just means fixing spelling

facts.fact: A single precise verb can often replace a weak verb plus an adverb: 'sprinted' says more than 'ran very quickly'.
facts.hook: a race scene that sounds slow until the verbs change

facts.fact: 'Very' plus a weak adjective can usually be swapped for one stronger word, such as 'exhausted' for 'very tired' or 'freezing' for 'very cold'.
facts.hook: a draft with 'very' on every line

facts.fact: Vague adjectives like 'nice', 'good' and 'interesting' give the writer's opinion without showing anything; a concrete detail lets the reader picture it and judge.
facts.hook: a grandparent asks what exactly was 'nice' about the trip

facts.fact: Stacked adjectives in English usually follow the order opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose, which is why 'a big red ball' sounds right and 'a red big ball' does not.
facts.hook: a friend learning English asks why one phrase sounds wrong

facts.fact: When every sentence is about the same length, writing tends to sound monotonous; mixing short and long sentences gives it rhythm.
facts.hook: a story that puts the whole class to sleep when read aloud

facts.fact: A short sentence placed after several long ones stands out, so writers often use one for the moment they most want the reader to notice.
facts.hook: the scary moment in a story finally lands after one cut

facts.fact: Reading a draft aloud often makes repeated rhythms and clumsy phrases easier to notice than reading it silently.
facts.hook: stumbling over one's own sentence while reading to the club

facts.fact: As a teenage reporter at the Kansas City Star, Ernest Hemingway learned from a style sheet that began 'Use short sentences. Use short first paragraphs.'
facts.hook: a club member tries writing a paragraph the Hemingway way

facts.fact: The Flesch Reading Ease test, created by Rudolf Flesch, scores how easy writing is to read using its average sentence length and average syllables per word.
facts.hook: a word processor rates a draft as hard to read
